title: Casper didn’t win on price or on the mattress
text: Medium Casper didn’t win on price or on the mattress | by Aryan Varma Sagi | Sep, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Medium Logo Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in What the showroom was actually selling The second half of the machine The wedge The part that complicates the victory lap What to take from this References Aryan Varma Sagi AI Product Manager | Solutions Architect | MS ASU Aryan Varma Sagi AI Product Manager | Solutions Architect | MS ASU Aryan Varma Sagi AI Product Manager | Solutions Architect | MS ASU Product Management Product Strategy Business Strategy Sales Ecommerce Casper didn’t win on price or on the mattress Aryan Varma Sagi 5 min read · Just now -- Listen Share Both explanations are standard but the showroom’s real product was never the bed. Press enter or click to view image in full size The story goes that Casper compressed a mattress into a box, shipped it to your door, cut out the middleman, and a $29 billion industry never recovered. Except Tuft & Needle had been doing exactly that since July 2012, nearly two years before Casper launched. Two software engineers started it with $6,000 of their own money and later a $500,000 loan. By the end of 2013, before Casper existed, they had done a million dollars in sales. By 2017 they were at $170 million, with a return rate of about 4 percent against an industry average near 11 percent. So the box was not the wedge. Somebody else shipped it first, cheaper, with better retention. What Casper removed was something else, and its founders were unusually direct about what. What the showroom was actually selling Philip Krim, Casper’s co-founder, described the incumbent mechanism plainly. “Mattress retailers play a game with eight gradients of firmness,” he said, and explained that this is how a customer gets guided across the floor toward something more expensive. Read that as a product decision rather than a complaint. Those eight gradients are not a response to eight distinct kinds of sleeper. They are rungs. Each one gives a salesperson a defensible reason to walk you one step up, because there is always a slightly better version of the thing you just liked. The floor plan is the funnel. The inventory is the script. And the compensation matched. Former Mattress Firm sales staff have described commissions tiered on margin rather than on price, with the percentage stepping down as margin falls. A salesperson steering you toward the higher-margin bed was not being predatory. They were reading their pay structure correctly, which is what people do. The second half of the machine A steering system only works if the customer cannot check the steering. This is where the industry’s strangest practice comes in, and it has a name inside the trade: the name game. Manufacturers sell the same or nearly the same mattress to different retailers under retailer-exclusive model names. Consumer Reports documented it in 2014. The purpose is not subtle and nobody involved pretends otherwise. If no competitor stocks the exact model you are looking at, no comparison is possible, and the low-price guarantee on the wall can be advertised indefinitely because it will never be triggered. Krim identified this too, saying the sprawl of retail options tends to “obscure the fact that the products are fundamentally the same.” Now put the two halves together, because separately they look like ordinary retail sleaze and together they are an engineered system. SKU proliferation gives the salesperson somewhere to steer you. Name exclusivity guarantees you cannot verify where you were steered. Margin-tiered commission supplies the motive. Those are not three bad habits. That is one product, and the mattress is not it. The product is a decision architecture that reliably converts an undecided shopper into a higher-margin purchase. The wedge Casper launched in April 2014 with one mattress, offered only in different sizes. The standard reading is that this was about simplicity, or about supply chain efficiency, or about a clean brand. Those are downstream effects. The structural consequence is sharper: a salesperson holding one product is not a salesperson. There is nothing to steer between, nothing to walk you up toward, no adjacent model whose name you cannot look up. Casper did not build a better showroom. It removed the showroom’s reason to exist, which is a different and much harder thing to counter. Mattress Firm could have matched the box in a quarter, and eventually legacy retailers did. It could not match one SKU without dismantling the mechanism that made its floor profitable. In October 2018, Mattress Firm filed for bankruptcy with more than 3,300 stores. The part that complicates the victory lap Casper is not a clean success story, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. The company posted about $439 million in revenue in 2019 against a net loss of roughly $93 million. It went public in 2020, was taken private in 2022, and was acquired in 2024 by Carpenter Co., a foam manufacturer. Along the way it expanded into multiple mattress models and opened its own physical stores, rebuilding both of the things it had originally removed. Meanwhile Tuft & Needle, which started with $6,000 and no venture backing, reached comparable scale on a fraction of the capital and sold to Serta Simmons in 2018. So the honest conclusion is not that one SKU is a moat. It plainly was not. Casper’s single mattress was a wedge, and a wedge is a tool for getting inside a category, not for holding one. What to take from this Two things, and the second is the uncomfortable one. First, when an incumbent looks irrational, check whether the irrationality is load-bearing. Eight firmness gradients and unreadable model names look like clutter until you notice they are the mechanism. The most defensible thing a competitor owns is often the thing that makes least sense from the outside, because that is the part nobody thinks to attack and nobody can copy with
